analysis.one_liner: Restricts PAC money, bundling, and out-of-district donations while easing limits on political parties.
analysis.headline: A House committee reported this campaign finance bill on a near-party-line 6-5 vote in July 1996, but the full House never voted on it before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the rules for financing federal elections. It would bar House candidates from taking more money from people outside their district than from inside it, cut PAC contribution limits to the same low level as individual donors, ban PACs and registered lobbyists from bundling checks, shut down leadership PACs run by members of Congress, and ban cash gifts over $100. It would also require campaigns to disclose late contributions within 24 hours and post reports on the internet. But it would simultaneously loosen limits elsewhere: raise contribution caps over time through inflation indexing, let individuals give more through political parties, let parties spend unlimited money communicating with a broadly defined set of "members," and let parties spend unlimited money against candidates who finance their own campaigns.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, voters would get faster disclosure of who is funding campaigns, House candidates would depend more on their own constituents than on out-of-district and PAC money, and small grassroots donors would get new protections against pressure and reprisals from the corporations and unions that solicit them.

how_it_helps.text: House candidates could not accept more in contributions from people outside their congressional district than from local residents, with penalties of three to five times the excess, and had to report the split in every filing.
PAC contributions to federal candidates and other committees would drop from the multi-candidate PAC level to the same limit that applies to individual donors.
PACs and anyone registered under the Lobbying Disclosure Act could no longer act as conduits or bundlers of contributions to federal candidates.
Federal candidates and officeholders could no longer establish or control political committees other than their own principal campaign committee, closing the leadership-PAC channel.
No candidate or committee could accept cash contributions totaling more than $100 from any person, and late contributions would have to be reported within 24 hours and posted on the Internet.

Corporations and unions could solicit all employees and members rather than only executives, but would have to protect the confidentiality of gifts of $100 or less and would face new penalties for forcing or retaliating against people over political contributions.

analysis.who_pays: Corporate and trade PACs, registered lobbyists who bundle donations, and members of Congress who use side leadership committees would lose major fundraising channels, while large donors would face new reporting within 24 hours of a gift.

drawbacks.text: The bill indexes every contribution limit to inflation starting in 1997, so the caps on money in politics would ratchet upward automatically rather than staying fixed.
It excludes contributions to political parties from an individual's overall cap and raises the limit for gifts to state parties, letting the same donor channel more money through party committees.

Parties could spend unlimited money on communications with "members," a definition broad enough to include anyone who voted in a party primary or ever gave the party a reportable contribution, and could use non-federal money for state and local party grassroots activity, which critics viewed as replacing one fundraising loophole with a larger one.

Political parties could make unlimited contributions to oppose a candidate who spends large amounts of personal money, effectively lifting limits in races involving wealthy self-funded candidates above $150,000.

The out-of-district rule applies only to House candidates, not Senate or presidential candidates, and by capping direct donations it could push more money toward party committees and independent spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The restrictions on PAC money, lobbyist bundling, leadership PACs, and out-of-district fundraising were real and would have made House members more answerable to their own constituents. But the bill gave with one hand and took with the other: indexed limits, looser party caps, unlimited party communications with a loosely defined membership, and unlimited party responses to self-funded candidates. Whether the net result reduced the influence of concentrated money or simply rerouted it through the parties was the central objection to the bill, and the record does not resolve it.

outcome.mechanism: The House Oversight Committee reported the bill 6-5 on July 16, 1996, and it sat on the Union Calendar until the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, without the full House ever voting on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Thomas introduced the bill on July 9, 1996, with nine original cosponsors including Speaker Gingrich, Majority Leader Armey, and Majority Whip DeLay, and it was referred to the House Committee on House Oversight.
The committee held a markup the next day and ordered the bill reported on a 6-5 roll-call vote on July 10, 1996.
The committee reported the bill with amendments on July 16, 1996, and it was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 349.
No further action appears in the record; the bill never reached the House floor and died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because no bill passed, the existing campaign finance rules carried into the 1996 elections unchanged. PACs, lobbyist bundlers, and large donors kept operating under the old limits, and political parties kept the soft-money channels the bill would have partially redirected.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Republican, the committee reported the bill on a 6-5 vote, and no Democrat attached their name to it.

industries.note: The bill would channel more money through party committees: party gifts excluded from donors' aggregate caps, higher limits for state parties, unlimited party spending on communications with a loosely defined membership, unlimited party money against self-funded candidates, and non-federal money for state and local party grassroots work. Even as it restricts direct giving, the bill would make parties the central conduit for large sums.
PAC contribution limits would drop to the individual-donor level and PAC bundling would be banned, sharply cutting a major corporate channel to House members.
Registered lobbyists could no longer bundle contributions for federal candidates, reducing their value to clients seeking access.

Corporations could solicit political contributions from all employees rather than only executives, but they would have to protect the confidentiality of gifts of $100 or less and face penalties for pressure or reprisals against employees.

Unions would gain the same broader solicitation authority as corporations, but the bill adds protections against physical force, job discrimination, and financial reprisals for coerced contributions, which serves union members directly.

Incumbents would lose leadership PACs, a favored side vehicle, but would gain inflation-indexed limits and a rule letting parties match an incumbent's carried-over war chest with unlimited contributions to a challenger.
